transcription.text: Thank you, everyone, and welcome back. This next session we will hear from policy makers
and from Stuart Charity from the Australian Automobile Aftermarket Association about policy
developments that have been happening here in Australia. First, Stuart was unable to
join us today, so we'll be giving an online presentation to us. So, Stuart Charity is
the CEO of the Australian Automobile Aftermarket Association, and that represents nearly 300
members and the broader $14 billion Australian automobile aftermarket industry. Stuart and the
AAAA has led the fight to tackle the aftermarket industry's largest issue, which was mandatory data
sharing. With a huge milestone being reached just last month with mandatory data sharing
legislation being introduced here in Australia, which is our first right to repair legislation
here in Australia. So, I would like to invite Stuart to present to you his industry's journey
on the right to repair. Thank you, Stuart.
Well, good morning, everyone. Just before I start, I'd like to congratulate the committee
of the Right to Repair Summit on this terrific initiative. I only wish that I could have been
in Canberra with you all today. Unfortunately, as it has many times over the last 14 months,
COVID's gotten away and we're unable to travel up to Canberra, but I look forward to
catching up with you all shortly live on the Q&A once the presentations are done.
Today, my presentation will be on the mandatory data sharing law that has now been introduced
and passed through the Australian Parliament. In fact, it passed the Australian Parliament
just a few weeks ago on the 17th of June and went through the House of Representatives eight
weeks before that during March. I'll talk a little bit about the operation of the
law in a tick, but essentially it's being enforced by the ACCC. In fact, there was a
budget allocation this year for nearly $10 million over five years. And there are significant
penalties for breach of the law. In fact, it's up to $10 million per company per breach. So
the law has a lot of teeth, which is fantastic. Now, I know, as I say, I won't go into a huge
amount of detail on the law today, but happy to take questions on it or send you follow-up
information and so on. Instead, I'll focus the majority of my presentation on our journey, because
this was a significant achievement. It's the first right to repair law in Australia.
And it was a 10-year journey. So it took us a decade to become an overnight success.
And there was a lot of hard work and a lot of learnings along the way. And I want to share
some of those with you today, because I think even though we'll talk about automotive repair
and service specifically, I think there are a lot of learnings in other sectors. And one of the
important things about this forum, I believe, is having other industry sectors being able to
leverage and share experiences. But before I do that, I just wanted to set the scene on why I
believe automotive repair and service was first cab off the rank with right to repair legislation
in Australia. And I fundamentally believe it's because of a number of reasons. One is that
the car is a unique consumer product. There's nothing like it in any other sector.
And it's because it's attributes. When you're buying a car, they're very expensive.
In fact, they're often the second largest purchase a family will make outside of their family
home. So quite a big capital investment. They're very technologically advanced, and I'll talk about
that in a tick. But they're also, they have some unique obligations as well. As you all know,
when you buy a brand new car, if you do not follow the manufacturer's specifications and service
schedule, then you essentially forfeit your consumer rights over that product. And
with most cars, there is a requirement to service that vehicle twice a year to maintain
your warranty on that vehicle and your consumer rights. The other area is that, and this is a
safety related area for the safety of you and your occupants, but also other road users,
there's a legal obligation to keep your car roadworthy. And again, requirements to make
sure that bald tires are replaced, that the headlights are fixed and so on. So that all
feeds into what is a very, very large market that we've got 18 million registered passenger
vehicles on Australian roads, times that by a couple of services a year and repairs and so on.
And it's a significant amount spent per household on car repair and maintenance. And
the entire industry itself is a $22 billion industry. So significant industry. In fact,
we believe and we're pretty confident that the automotive repair and service industry would be
the biggest repair industry in Australia by far. So that's certainly one factor why we're here
today with an industry specific set of competition laws. The other one, as I said at the outset,
is around technology on vehicles. This slide is a few years old now, it's 10 years old and
anything to do with technology, 10 years is like an eternity. But even back 10 years ago,
11 years ago in 2010, the average passenger vehicle at that time had more lines of code
on it than a 787 Dreamliner and an F-35 Joint Strike Fighter. So these are sophisticated
pieces of machinery and they're becoming increasingly computerised. In fact, from about
2010 onwards and certainly model year 2012 onwards, the uptake of technology on vehicles
has just been exponential. And whilst that technology has created a lot of benefits,
cars are a lot safer, they're a lot more economical and so on, they have a lot more
features on them now. But what that's done by embedding all that technology into the vehicle,
it's given the car manufacturers a very, very powerful mechanism to be able to manipulate the
market. And being large multinational companies that are trying to make as much profit as they
can, they've certainly taken advantage of that. So what are the barriers to repair in the car
industry? Well, they're numerous and the car companies are very, because as I said, they're
controlling that technology and they've got access to a huge market. So they're highly motivated to
try and work every way they can to manipulate the market and to maximise their profits.
One of the things that I'll harp on in terms of learnings, we've done a lot of
research and surveys and other information that we've been able to present to government and the
regulators to substantiate our position over the years. But one pretty significant one was a survey
that we did in 2016. It was a time when the ICCC were conducting a market study into the new car
retailing industry. And we went out and surveyed thousands of workshops to find out exactly where
they were struggling and what the impact was. And the main area is that it can be as simple as
the oil blend. Service and repair on a vehicle is completely different to service and repair when
we were all growing up with a lot of do it yourself. You could go and buy a repair manual
down at your, a hard copy repair manual down at your local auto store. But now a lot of the
features on the vehicle are all computerised and so on. So I talked about oil blend. You wouldn't
think that to be a state secret, but that was really, really difficult to get and many repairers
weren't able to get it. And it could be catastrophic if you put the wrong oil
in a vehicle, you'll blow the engine and the repairer will be liable for it. And what we saw
from about 2016 onwards is car companies starting to put in the owner's manual in your glove box
under oil specification, they'd put, refer to dealer. Of course, when you ring up the dealer,
the dealer says, oh, we can't give out that information. It's intellectual property. You'll
have to bring the car in. So you ask your repairer, can you get the oil for me from the dealer? The
repairer rings a dealer, dealer says, oh, we don't sell that in retail packs. You have to tell the
customer to bring the car in. That's a very simple way of withholding information and manipulating
the market. And certainly the car companies have used that, but it's a lot more sophisticated than
that. The repair process now involves some scan tools. So first thing a repairer will do when
your car comes in is not start pulling it apart. They'll hook it up to a scan tool and the car
will self-diagnose and tell the technician what, they'll release it. The car will put up a whole
lot of fault codes if there's something wrong. And then that allows the technician to be able
to diagnose, repair the fault, and then clear the codes. Problem is that the car companies
are controlling that process now. So they're not providing information to be able to diagnose what
the codes are. Often the codes will be grayed out and so on. So that's creating huge issues.
Also, we're increasingly seeing that when we're replacing, when technicians are replacing parts
on vehicles, they're required to put in an initialization code, might be an eight-digit code
or whatever. Again, that can only be done from the dealership or by the dealership. And the dealer
has to have the car physically in their lot. So what we were seeing and what we're
increasingly seeing is a repairer who's qualified, has all the tools, and has experienced staff and
so on, undertaking repair, getting right to the end, and then finding that they can't restart the vehicle
because they haven't got the code. So then they're having to put a vehicle on a flatbed truck and
send it to a dealership to get a code put in. And often that dealership will make them wait a week
or two weeks. Waste of money, waste of productivity, and makes the repairer look
bad in front of their customer for no reason. And the final thing we're seeing increasingly is
similar to your iPhone, car companies will do tweaks on vehicles or upgrade the
systems on a vehicle through a reflash of the software. Again though, they only send that
information about the reflashing out to their dealership networks and completely avoid the
independent repairers. And often they'll be sending out technical bulletins only to
their dealerships. So an independent repairer might spend four hours troubleshooting a fault
that's a known fault and there's a known fix from the vehicle manufacturer. Often they won't pass
that on to the customer, but it's a waste of productivity and so on. Back in 2016, when we
did that survey, one in 10 vehicles experienced issues around getting information. And on average
it took four hours and hundreds of dollars in costs for the repairer to be able to access that
information. That was back in 2016. We estimate that it would be one in two, one in three vehicles
now. And it was increasing exponentially as the technology on vehicles was increasing. So
something had to be done. I talked earlier about the ACCC and this is what was done. We and others
lobbied for the ACCC to investigate what was going on in the industry. And one thing the ACCC do very
well is they follow the money. And in this new car market study, that's exactly what they did.
And this slide in front of you shows that whilst we've established that the car company have the
technological power to be able to manipulate the market, this shows the why. Why would they do it?
As I said, a $22 billion industry and this is straight out of the ACCC market study. And what
it shows is that the average gross margin on service in a dealership is 64%. 21% on parts,
that's fairly reasonable, but it's a 64% that really stands out. But the other figure that
really stands out here is this is a new car dealer. Look at the margins they make on a new car,
7%. It's almost, this reminds me a lot of the inkjet printer industry, that the
printer's almost the lost leader and they make all their money selling you the cartridges of
the coffee machines, similar. So this is what alerted the ACCC to the fact that there was a
problem in our industry. And they looked at this, they looked at the margins and you extrapolate
that out on the overall turnover of the industry. You look at the technological advantage they have
and the commercial imperative they have, and the ACCC quite rightly found that there was a
market failure here and that it wasn't going to resolve itself. And because it was causing
a loss of competition and consumer detriment, that there was a role for government to play
in regulating the industry. So we got our legislation as a direct result of that ACCC
recommendation. And essentially the legislation is an amendment to the Competition and Consumer Act.
It's the first one that's ever been done for a specific industry. So there's a set of specific
competition rules governing our industry now. So the legislation itself, even though it has
gone through Parliament and it is law, it will be fully operational from the 1st of July 2022. So
there's essentially a 12-month phasing. I won't go into a lot of detail on the legislation, but
essentially it's principles-based and we support that. So it talks a lot about what you're not
allowed to do. And most importantly, car companies are not allowed to withhold information that they
would normally share with their authorised dealer networks. They're not allowed to withhold
that to independent repairers. They must provide it in the same form, same function, in the same
timelines that they do with their independent repairers. And importantly, the scheme design
includes an industry body and that industry body will play a key role in operationalising the
scheme. So they will provide the function of educating the industry on what information is
available and where to get it. They'll manage a dispute resolution and monitoring service.
They'll report back to the government on the operation of the scheme and make recommendations
on how the scheme may be tweaked to make it more effective. And they'll also run a secure
data release model to make sure that any security-related information is protected
and traceable. And that's really important because we know that one of the things that the car
industry were trying to push is that they need to hold on to anything that's security or safety
related. And if they had a basic agreement from the government to do that, they would have tied
everything to security and safety. And it's logical, anything on a vehicle could be tied to
safety. So they have to share security-related information. Now, this information is not free.
Repairers have to pay for it, but it's on fair and reasonable commercial terms.
And there is a very comprehensive definition in the legislation of what that means.
And it includes benchmarks to similar information in other markets.
And I think one of the most important things is that it gives the flexibility
for the minister of the day to make changes to the legislation, all the scheme rules,
if they identify that there are activities underway that are designed to frustrate the scheme.
And they're the exact words. So if car companies start finding loopholes in the scheme,
then the minister of the day has the ability to close those loopholes. That's really important.
That feature and that reporting loop back from that industry association on the operation of
the scheme and recommendations mean that the government has the flexibility to change things
as they go, because we are in a technology-driven environment and the technology is changing.
So the scheme will need to be able to change. So it's essentially future-proofed.
And the final thing I think is welcome news for many of you, because I know a lot of you aren't
from the automotive industry. The government has designed this legislation as basically the
forerunner for right to repair legislation in other, or schemes in other sectors.
It's essentially designed so that they can piggyback straight onto this legislation.
And I'm being followed by someone from the ACCC. There's been a lot of activity around
agricultural equipment. And I think the ACCC have flagged that that might be another sector
that could be added onto this down the track. But essentially it could, the scheme could be
adapted and for many, many other sectors. So that's certainly welcome news for everyone.
This is a slide that we like to use. This is the kind of David and Goliath battle that we've been
taking on. And I wanted to talk now a little bit more about our journey and share with you some
of the insights and some of the learnings that we've had over those, over that long 10 years.
And make no mistake, the car industry are one of the most powerful and influential lobby groups
going around. They've, you know, they've got lawyers at a thousand paces. They're very,
very well financed and they're very good at getting their own way. So we've come up against
them and we've won out in this case. But there's been a lot of steps to it. And I wanted to give
you really just narrow it down to what I think were the key reasons why we got the outcome we did.
First of all, we were very, very clear that this was a consumer issue. This was about the consumer's
right to choose who repairs their vehicle and what parts are fitted on it. In fact, our tagline for
the campaign was your car, your choice. So we believe you buy the car, you should be able to
have it repaired anywhere you like. And that repairer should have all the information they
need to be able to conduct that repair effectively. We could have run a whole lot of lines.
Our industry consists of 25,000 predominantly small family-owned businesses. So we could have
run the small business angle, you know, going up against the multinational car companies.
You know, we could have run on the economic input that our industry make. We could have
very legitimately run on the environment. If you create a situation where cars can be
conveniently and economically serviced regularly, that's great for the environment from an emissions
point of view, from a fuel economy point of view. Well-maintained cars last longer. So
you don't need as many new cars on the road. So there's a whole lot of environmental angles and
so on, and they're all legitimate, but we kept it to the consumer angle. We did use some of those
other arguments at the appropriate time, but we kept it to the one portfolio for two reasons.
One is that as we got, once we got the ACCC recommendation that this was, this situation
was creating consumer detriment and that it was only going to get worse, that was very,
very powerful. And the government really had no option but to act on that. So we were able to get
a lever, a mechanism to essentially force the government's hand to act. The other thing we
found with government relations, if you try and spread the message too wide, what you do is you
end up going across different portfolios. So in the example that I used, you know, we mainly were
dealing with the treasurer and the assistant treasurer in the competition portfolios, but if
you start going into environment and it's a small business and so on, what happens is that it becomes
no one's problem then. If multiple ministers have responsibility, then they can leave it to the other
one. So you find that things stall. So having that very tight message and very clear, and we think
if there are competition issues, that that's the optimum thing to run on.
The second piece of advice that we would give is anticipate the pushback. Now we were really
fortunate that, and I think there's the characteristics that I'll be talking about
now are shared across most of your industry sectors. Most of the companies that are engaging
in anti-competitive behaviour, it's fair to say, are large multinational companies.
And they're hard to take on because they've got deep pockets and they're very powerful, as I said,
but their Achilles heel is that they operate in the same way in different markets. And the right
to repair in the automotive has been going on all around the world and continues to go on to this
day. So we had the benefit, I guess, of hindsight of being able to hook up with all of our sister
associations around the world and share market intel on what the car industry were going to say
and what arguments they were going to run even before they ran them. And that put us in such
an advantageous position. To give you an example, as we launched the campaign to parliamentarians,
we actually had a brochure. I don't know whether you can see that, but it's got excuses and answers.
So car servicing and consumer choice, the top car industry excuses. So we're already
telling them that they'll say that this is about stealing the IP on vehicles. It's about
security and safety. It's about technician safety. If they're not trained properly,
then they're going to kill themselves if you give them the information. The last one's a doozy,
that independent repairers will steal their customers' cars if you give them information.
That just doesn't make any sense at all. It's a pretty short-term business model,
I would have thought. We have heard all the excuses, but we were ready for the car industry
and we had responses to those excuses before they'd even made them.
So this, I believe, was the game changer. Finding a way or a better way to explain your issue.
One of the really difficult car industry excuses that we really had trouble countering was they
were saying there is no problem. All the information's out there. How can there be a
problem when you've got 25,000 independent repairers out there? They service 60% of the
market. So what's the problem? They must be getting the information. So where's the issue?
The issue, obviously, was in the detail and it was getting worse, as I said. But how do you
articulate that to members of parliament to engender them to act on it? It's very difficult
to do it when you're sitting in their offices, in parliament house, when there's lobbyist after
lobbyist going through like a revolving door, all with their legitimate issues and trying to
push their positions and whatever. So we made the decision, and I think this was a groundbreaking
decision. We flipped that on its head. Instead of us going to Canberra and doing the rounds,
and we did all of that, but what we did was actually engage our members. Our members that
were small businesses out there in every electorate in Australia, and we encouraged them to write to
their local members of parliament and invite them into their workshop. And that was absolutely
incredible. The response we got from our members was absolutely amazing. We had hundreds and
hundreds of them write to their local members of parliament. We actually hosted 75 federal MP
visits to workshops all around the country. And I tell you, those members of parliament, they love
it. They love coming into a workshop in their local constituency and meeting with real people.
And our members were amazing. The way they articulated what the issue was, how it impacted
on their business and the future of their business, but most importantly, how it impacted on their
customers, which were all constituents of these electorates. And I tell you, not one of them came
out of those workshops in any doubt about the issue and about the need for action. And that is
why our legislation sailed through the parliament. In fact, there were two hours of debates from all
sides of parliament supporting the legislation. So we had unanimous support and it was because
of this grassroots campaign. So what did we learn along the way? Well, from our industry perspective,
banding together makes us very, very strong and we can take on the most powerful,
one of the most powerful lobby groups in any industry sector and win because we're stronger
together and we're stronger than we think. And I believe we're stronger as a right to repair
community. And we're very, very keen now that we've got this legislation through to assist
other sectors in our learning so that we can all be stronger together. That engagement model,
that grassroots engagement by our independent repair workshops was just incredible. The impact
that it had on members of parliament, but also the loyalty, like we essentially brought them into
our campaign and made them part of it. And the loyalty that we're enjoying now is
incredible. So if you are a membership association or whatever, or you're part of an
industry that has one, bring the industry together through your industry association
and have faith in each other and back each other and you'll be amazed at the results you can get.
One of the things that I've always said is that I've always been glad that I've been on this
side of the fence because we're actually telling the truth. I'd hate to be the car industry lobby
being told what arguments you got to run and having to basically make it up as you go.
So it's easy to be on point and it's easy to be consistent when you're actually telling the truth.
And the final thing to say is that you have to have evidence and data and they're different. So
we had to have, in our case, we had to have make, model, time of day, workshop, what the issue was
and so on down to that level. But we also had to have that high level data to show that
there was a systemic issue. And we had to have persistence. Wow, Leslie Yates, our
relations manager and I, 10 years of our lives, and that wasn't the only thing we were
working on, but 10 years of our lives, so many trips to Canberra, so many workshop visits, so
many letters, and we just kept going. And we knew how important this was and we knew that
failure wasn't an option because it would have basically spelt death by a thousand cuts
for our great industry. So we just kept doggedly going on and so on. And in the end,
we got the result. And probably one of the proudest moments I've had is, as the legislation
went through the House of Representatives, Andrew Lee, the Shadow Assistant Treasurer,
had just got off his feet and after, I think, five of his Labor colleagues had all supported
the legislation. And I sent him a text message to thank him for everything he did, the
opposition and the government both were tremendously supportive of this. But I sent
this text to Andrew Lee and he responded and said, your association set the benchmark
for advocacy. You're polite, you're doggedly determined, and you're fact-based. And I think
that's the best compliment we can get. I'll end with a quote from David Glythe
and we very much believe this was a David and Glythe battle. The car companies could outspend
us, but we had grit and we just kept going and going and going. And in the end, we got over the
line. Now, the funny thing is that this is a pretty historic moment, but this is not the end
of the war. We might have won that battle, but it's not the end of the war. And a lot of people
say to me, now you've got this, what are you going to do now? I can tell you the technology's moving
on. The car industry aren't going to sit on their hands. They'll have to cop this, but they're
already working on telematics, which is wirelessly connected vehicles and a whole lot of other things
to try and lock us out into the future. And we'll keep going. We're now emboldened by this,
but we will keep going. And ultimately, truth and consistency and effort will overcome even the most
powerful lobby groups. So can I just finish today by expressing our gratitude to the entire
right to repair community and specifically to Professor Leanne Wiseman, who has been
absolutely tremendous success to us, support to us. She's written numerous submissions
in support of our campaign and has been a great advocate for change in our sector.
And we do feel part of this community. We're facing many of the same issues and we're fighting
against the same vested commercial interests that will try and prevent our ability to repair,
reuse and repurpose. And we're proud to belong to this community. And I'm really grateful for the
opportunity to share our journey. Thank you very much. And I look forward to taking some questions
during the Q&A session. Thank you. Thank you very much, Stuart. It's fantastic to hear the journey
that the AAAA and I would just like to apologise and make a correction. It is the Australian
Automotive Aftermarket Association, which is the AAAA. And they in fact have 2,600 member companies.
So I'd like to just correct that. Next, I would like to invite Mark Labert from the ACCC to come
along. Mark is the Director of the Agricultural Unit. And the reason we have Mark speaking to us
today is that the Agricultural Unit has just released this year their final report into the
Agricultural Machinery After Sales Market Inquiry that they've conducted. And Mark, I'll hand it over
to you. Thank you very much. Thanks very much, Leanne. And good morning, all. So it's a real
pleasure to be able to speak to you today about our market study into agricultural machinery
markets. So I'd really just like to thank Leanne and her team as well for the organisation of this
event, obviously persevering through great difficulty to be able to put this together
in such an amazing agenda and program. So I really appreciate your efforts in that as well.
So I'm Mark Labert and I'm a Director in the ACCC's Agriculture Unit.
So just a bit of background about me. I've been at the ACCC for approximately 11 years,
working across a number of different areas. But over the last five to six years,
primarily in the agriculture space. And part of our work is doing really deep dive work in
agriculture markets to explore competition and fair trading issues. So that's been a key part
of our work. And one of the most recent projects that we've undertaken was our study into agricultural
machinery. So interestingly, our findings led to recommendations that link quite closely with
the motor vehicle scheme that Stuart's just discussed, but also the broader right to repair
work that's happening that Paul will discuss afterwards. So I think this presentation is
neatly wedged between the two and appropriately so. So just quickly before I dive into the specifics
of our market study, I think it's worth just broadly touching on the ACCC's role and how
that interrelates with right to repair issues. So for those particularly outside the country,
the ACCC is Australia's national competition, consumer protection and fair trading regulator.
So we're an independent statutory authority. So in that sense, independent from government,
we are not a policy body. So ultimately, it's, of course, the government to make policy.
But through these processes, we do make recommendations,
particularly in relation to market issues that from time to time, obviously, government adopts
to address the issues that we identify as part of our studies.
I think one of the key things in our role and one of our overall broader objectives
as an organisation is promoting and maintaining competition. So one of the really emerging issues
that we're seeing is, well, how do we promote and maintain competition in after sales markets?
So that's something that's been, I guess, an emerging feature in the work that we've done.
So Stuart touched upon, I think, one of the initial projects in this area that we undertook,
which was our 2017 car retailing market study. And I won't go through that in detail today,
but it just highlights that this is an emerging issue that the ACCC is engaging with.
Obviously, our recommendation in this space was taken forward by government,
and the ACCC has been very pleased to see that occur. And that's something where in these market
studies, we're really diving down into the issues and looking at the really competition and fair
trading issues that are impacting the markets overall. I think critical to recognise that
that's our objective. We're here to look at the efficiency of markets. So the ACCC, I guess,
doesn't have a horse in the race, if I can put it in those terms. We're really looking at the
markets overall. So Stuart also touched upon the fact that the ACCC has an ongoing role in relation
to the motor vehicle scheme. And I won't recover the ground that Stuart comprehensively addressed
today in his presentation. But I think I just wanted to quickly highlight that we do have a
team focused on this work going forward. Obviously, very early days with the scheme just coming into
force, but something where our team in that area will be engaging and consulting closely with
people going forward on those particular issues. So it's an important and exciting new piece of
work for the ACCC. So just jumping into the market study. So I think we really commenced
this market study as actually an offline, really small research project. So it was something where
in undertaking that initial research, we realised, you know, actually, there's some
really significant issues here at play, some issues that needed to be explored further.
And what we also realised is that there is substantial stakeholder interest in this particular
market, and the issues emerging from issues, particularly in agricultural machinery after
sales markets. So in February 2020, we released a discussion paper, which basically set out some
initial views on these particular issues, and went out to industry to seek perspectives. And
obviously, as we always do with these issues, we received a wide range of different perspectives
from industry stakeholders. So we received 44 submissions, and they covered a really good
spectrum of the different components of the supply chain, and also people, academics and
people outside the supply chain who were able to offer some really valuable insights.
So I think another really important component of what we did here as well was we actually went to
the purchasers themselves. So with the support of a number of agriculture industry associations,
we were able to quite heavily promote a purchaser survey. It was quite a detailed survey, because
it really wanted us to get down to a granular level of detail that we could explore these
particular issues. So we had 335 responses to that particular survey, which we found to be
a good result given the challenges facing time poor farm businesses.
So our final report was released on the 4th of May in 2021. And obviously, I'll speak to the
findings and recommendations of that report today. So I think one thing that is worth highlighting,
just as you consider these points is that in this particular market study, I think the issues around
right to repair and the motor vehicle scheme were really, I guess, where we landed on,
not where we started. So we were looking at these issues broadly, we were looking at primary market
issues as well. So not all of the focus on our work was in relation to right to repair issues
from the start. But obviously, as our analysis progressed, we realised that the key concerns
from market participants were around those after sales markets issues. So that's ultimately where
a lot of our more major recommendations were directed. So it's been great that there's already
been a bit of discussion about agricultural machinery today. So I think in some respects,
this kind of question has already been answered. But just to flesh it out a little bit, I mean,

Well, I think there's two issues here. So I'll deal with the warranty issue first. So warranties
are obviously a voluntary contractual agreement entered into between two parties. So ultimately,
under Australian law as it currently stands, basically the setter of the warranty can
identify what those terms and conditions are. So you'll be subject to those terms and conditions
in a particular warranty that you enter into. The point I would probably highlight here,
and Paul did make this point, is that the consumer guarantees will also apply. So these
are statutory protections. You cannot contract out of those protections. It's actually a breach
of the Australian Consumer Law to indicate that those particular protections don't apply. So I
think that that's really critical in terms of the education piece, but also just in terms of
getting that message out more broadly that those protections are going to apply where the consumer
guarantees operate. So I think two distinct issues, but important to kind of be aware of
the way that they both operate. Thank you. Okay, next question. Is insurance going to be

consumer guarantee statutory rights that operate in parallel. And there's a lot of focus, too much
focus, we believe, on manufacturer's warranties and particularly where they're conditional.
The simple fact is that an independent repairer from a mechanical workshop point of view is
required to provide goods and services and essentially to warrant those. So if you take your
parts from an independent repairer and they don't repair it correctly or the part fails or so on,

that results as a result of that. Where there's some complications or confusion is that
manufacturers aren't able to condition their manufacturer's warranties, but often they will
tell car owners that if you take your car to an independent repairer or use so-called non-genuine
parts, then you void your warranty. That's actually illegal to say that. They cannot do that and they
can't enforce it. So I think there is an education piece there for consumers that they do have
statutory rights, whether they go to an independent or independent repairer.
